candidates.what_they_do: Contract chemical manufacturer in Valdosta, Georgia. Custom formulating, milling, blending, filling, packaging, warehousing and logistics for agricultural and pest control customers. Three facilities, 361,500 square feet, founded 1997.
candidates.employees: approximately 200, per the NIST MEP success story page fetched this run
candidates.bottleneck: Printed batch sheets. With more than 200 different customers, each sending non-standard data, staff burned hours every week hand-processing printed batch sheets, and the company had no systematic data collection behind it.
candidates.build: Two separate things, and that is the problem with this candidate. (1) dataPARC real-time data historian and visualisation software across two facilities, selected and implemented starting March 2022 with GaMEP's Industry 4.0 team, plus a new quality management system after a three-day quality assessment in June 2022. (2) Separately and later, a partnership with an AI vendor named on the page as Vieaura to test generative AI that converts printed batch sheets into a standardised digital format. The page describes item 2 as testing, with more than 100 batch sheets still to be converted.
candidates.pattern_id: P1 (document and intake) for the generative AI piece; the disclosed numbers actually belong to a data historian and quality project, which is closer to P8 plus ordinary Industry 4.0 instrumentation

ladder_rung.why: The batch sheet piece is a single model call turning a messy printed document into structured fields, with people checking it. It is not multi step, it does not use tools, it does not plan. And per the page it was still in testing, not production. The results that carry dollar figures came from data visualisation and quality work, which is rung 1 to 2 at most.

named_human.quote: GaMEP is a great asset for short-term and long-term goals. They help you think about the future and align yourself to reach those goals.

candidates.limit_named_by_source: The source itself says the generative AI batch sheet conversion is being tested and that more than 100 printed batch sheets are still to be converted into digital workflows. It never claims the AI produced any of the dollar figures.
candidates.skepticism_why: Three separate problems. First, attribution: the $30,000 a month, the 51 percent PONC cut and the 20 percent capacity gain are presented alongside the AI story but the page ties them to a data historian and a quality management project, not to the generative AI. Shipping them as an AI result would be exactly the inflation pattern EVIDENCE.md calls the narrow task, wide claim. Second, the AI was in testing, which is the demo-that-never-left-the-demo tell. Third, the work happened in 2022 and the page is dated 2024, so the tooling economics are stale for a 2026 decision. Also worth flagging for the verifier: the GaMEP mirror of this story at gamep.org returned an empty body on fetch, so a second independent read of the same facts has not been achieved, and my read of the NIST page came back through the fetch summariser rather than as raw text. Every number above needs to be found verbatim in the page before it goes anywhere near an artifact.
candidates.why_dana_cares: A 200 person contract manufacturer whose people hand-processed printed customer paperwork every week is exactly Dana's back office, but the receipts here belong to a data project, not to the AI, so it does not yet teach Dana anything true about AI.
candidates.verdict_why: Passes size, ordinariness, named bottleneck, disclosed cost, disclosed timeline and a named human. Fails filter 4 because no number is attributable to the AI, fails the production test because the AI was in testing, fails the agentic mandate at rung 3, and the underlying work is 2022. Worth an interview to find out whether the batch sheet conversion reached production, what that specific piece cost, and what the before and after on batch sheet handling time actually was. Not shippable as written.

ground_notes: Honest read: this ground did not deliver this run. The cost half of the hard gate is real here — MEP success stories carry an impact box that routinely includes a New Investment dollar figure, and they almost always end with a named client quote. That is two of the seven filters handed over for free. But the AI supply is close to zero. The whole NIST MEP success story index for 2025 and 2026 contains no title touching AI, artificial intelligence, machine learning or software; the stories are ISO certification, lean, value stream mapping, additive, ExporTech and e-commerce. The only AI story the national network promotes is CJB Industries, dated 2024 about 2022 work, and NIST reuses it in at least three places, which is why it returned on every query. State centre AI pages are workshops, navigators, readiness assessments and blog explainers, not deployments. STOP DOING: querying MEP plus AI plus a year (converges on CJB every time); querying MEP centre domains for AI case studies with dollar figures until roughly mid 2027, when the 14 new NIST advanced-technology centre awards announced July 2026 have produced written outcomes. Grant announcement pages are structurally useless: all future tense, which is why FuzeHub and Michigan Industry 4.0 both died on filter 4. TRY NEXT TIME, in confidence order: (1) invert the MEP query — search the impact language MEP stories are written in, 'cost savings' plus 'new investment' plus an operator noun like 'batch sheets', 'work orders', 'quotes', 'scheduling', and let the AI turn up incidentally inside a story filed under process improvement; (2) state MEP annual and impact reports as PDFs rather than web case study pages, extracted with pypdf per EVIDENCE.md — the web pages are marketing, the PDFs carry client impact survey numbers; (3) Manufacturing PA Innovation Program, manufacturingpa.org/projects by region and year 2018 to 2025, carrying company plus university partner plus grant amount (public cost by law); the index page is empty so fetch the year pages directly; risk is that these are R&D partnerships so the named human and the operational before and after will usually be missing; (4) MGMA is a dead end for cases and live only for framing, their 2025 and 2026 Stat polls are aggregate survey data with zero named practices, and their March 2026 poll on phone bottlenecks was sponsored by an AI vendor; (5) untried and most promising: DOE Better Plants Better Project award submissions, written by operators for peers and carrying project cost and payback as a matter of format, plus rural electric co-op board packets and annual reports which disclose approved contract amounts, plus state office of rural health case studies. The reader-filter caution held exactly: every well documented public sector AI deployment was an agency Dana cannot be, and every private mid-market firm named by a government source came with the cost disclosed and the outcome missing, or the outcome disclosed and the AI attribution broken.
